## O — Customer Experience & Service

### O.1 — Voice of Customer Programs

**O.1.01 — Voice of Customer Programs Operating Model for operating signal**
*Summary:* An operating model pattern for voice of customer programs that explains how the operating signal shapes retail performance beyond generic channel or product analysis.
*Mechanism:* In practice, the retailer translates voice of customer programs into governance cadence, accountable owners, escalation paths, and cross-functional rituals; the useful artifact is a decision table that separates enterprise rules from cluster, category, channel, and partner exceptions.
*Decision relevance:* CXOs use this pattern during seasonal reset to decide whether a modernization, sourcing, AI, growth, margin, or resilience initiative has enough economic proof to scale across banners and channels.
*Pitfalls:* The common failure mode is treating vendor tooling as a strategy instead of an operating-model change; the mitigation is to force a before/after control, owner, metric grain, and exception path before funding the next tranche.
*Industry exemplars:* European grocery and hard-discount tiers typically expose this pattern through anonymized peer ranges such as basis-point margin movement, conversion lift, shrink movement, labor minutes per transaction, inventory turns, service-level deltas, or repeat-rate movement rather than through a single brand anecdote.
*Cross-references:* O.1.02; retail-v1:O; O.1; operating-model

**O.1.02 — Voice of Customer Programs Unit Economics for economic driver**
*Summary:* A unit economics pattern for voice of customer programs that explains how the role of economic driver shapes retail performance beyond generic channel or product analysis.
*Mechanism:* In practice, the retailer translates voice of customer programs into margin, cost-to-serve, working capital, and customer lifetime value tradeoffs; the useful artifact is a decision table that separates enterprise rules from cluster, category, channel, and partner exceptions.
*Decision relevance:* CXOs use this pattern during weekly operating review to decide whether a modernization, sourcing, AI, growth, margin, or resilience initiative has enough economic proof to scale across banners and channels.
*Pitfalls:* The common failure mode is optimizing the visible KPI while moving cost, inventory, labor, or risk elsewhere; the mitigation is to force a before/after control, owner, metric grain, and exception path before funding the next tranche.
*Industry exemplars:* specialty apparel and beauty leaders typically expose this pattern through anonymized peer ranges such as basis-point margin movement, conversion lift, shrink movement, labor minutes per transaction, inventory turns, service-level deltas, or repeat-rate movement rather than through a single brand anecdote.
*Cross-references:* O.1.01, O.1.03; retail-v1:O; O.1; unit-economics

*Mechanism:* In practice, the retailer translates store associate workforce strategy into governance cadence, accountable owners, escalation paths, and cross-functional rituals; the useful artifact is a decision table that separates enterprise rules from cluster, category, channel, and partner exceptions.
*Decision relevance:* CXOs use this pattern during seasonal reset to decide whether a modernization, sourcing, AI, growth, margin, or resilience initiative has enough economic proof to scale across banners and channels.
*Pitfalls:* The common failure mode is treating vendor tooling as a strategy instead of an operating-model change; the mitigation is to force a before/after control, owner, metric grain, and exception path before funding the next tranche.
*Industry exemplars:* European grocery and hard-discount tiers typically expose this pattern through anonymized peer ranges such as basis-point margin movement, conversion lift, shrink movement, labor minutes per transaction, inventory turns, service-level deltas, or repeat-rate movement rather than through a single brand anecdote.
*Cross-references:* P.1.02; retail-v1:P; P.1; operating-model

**P.1.02 — Store Associate Workforce Strategy Unit Economics for economic driver**
*Summary:* A unit economics pattern for store associate workforce strategy that explains how the role of economic driver shapes retail performance beyond generic channel or product analysis.
*Mechanism:* In practice, the retailer translates store associate workforce strategy into margin, cost-to-serve, working capital, and customer lifetime value tradeoffs; the useful artifact is a decision table that separates enterprise rules from cluster, category, channel, and partner exceptions.
*Decision relevance:* CXOs use this pattern during weekly operating review to decide whether a modernization, sourcing, AI, growth, margin, or resilience initiative has enough economic proof to scale across banners and channels.
*Pitfalls:* The common failure mode is optimizing the visible KPI while moving cost, inventory, labor, or risk elsewhere; the mitigation is to force a before/after control, owner, metric grain, and exception path before funding the next tranche.
*Industry exemplars:* specialty apparel and beauty leaders typically expose this pattern through anonymized peer ranges such as basis-point margin movement, conversion lift, shrink movement, labor minutes per transaction, inventory turns, service-level deltas, or repeat-rate movement rather than through a single brand anecdote.
*Cross-references:* P.1.01, P.1.03; retail-v1:P; P.1; unit-economics

*Mechanism:* In practice, the retailer translates workforce scheduling & optimization into customer, product, store, market, supplier, or channel clusters requiring different playbooks; the useful artifact is a decision table that separates enterprise rules from cluster, category, channel, and partner exceptions.
